paragraphs: Thanks, will study it
Well, I've finished vibe-coding our analytics system.

It can now pull literally all the data out of Instantly and perform analytical miracles with it, sending it when it's needed to where it's needed. All that's left is to bolt on invoice mechanics that will automatically invoice clients and automatically track payment on those invoices, plus some LLAMA to reason for free over trickier queries to the database than what's hard-wired — the ultra-weird rare “think about this” requests that are just dumb to turn into a hard-coded lever.
The whole thing took about 40 hours of vibe-coding.

Over these couple of projects that work not for fun but for real business (money moves = business is real), I understood not just in theory but felt in every cell of my body how pointless it is these days to start anything in the SaaS category.

Even over these couple of months of vibe-coding, everything has jumped a hundred miles ahead, and today coding without skills is several times easier than it was two months ago. The models simply can do more, think smarter, err less often, lay down more padding, and demand less pedantry in how you word the request.

As before, I maintain that somewhere during 2026 code will write itself. Nobody will … care about its quality, because these are projects “for yourself,” not for others. For an entrepreneur building for himself, the main thing is that the button clicks. For some tasks it's enough that it “at least sometimes clicks on the third try.”

The future belongs to business models that can actually do something in the physical world. The digital world is being taken away from entrepreneurs for good. Today there are still these arguments about whether it will keep getting smarter or not. But it will, and then even the ultra-complex projects you can't vibe-code today will lose their main property — the multiple-based valuation. And as the practice of ordinary startups from the year before last shows, losing valuation for a startup is like losing blood for an organism. Such an object flies out of the venture scheme and the wolves tear it apart. It still lives for a while, of course, but that's not life, it's meaningless existence.
People who want to create something are poor …, like me, by the way
People richer than some very small X all do business only to get richer, and creation comes bundled in, sometimes
It cracks me up that most people who don't do business actually don't understand what money is at all, can't count it whatsoever.
I had a guy in sales whom I once, by coincidence, asked: what's your dream? Because he'd mentioned he was moving toward a dream.
And he said he wanted to earn 300 thousand dollars in cash and thereby secure his children's lives forever
How he arrived at that math on a $5k-a-month salary, given that on that kind of money he obviously couldn't afford anything luxurious, was and remains a mystery to me
Today I was riding an escalator in a mall — I ran in — and thought about this yet again
People don't understand what a million dollars is
Or what ten is.
When your company makes a million dollars you can't even afford to give people New Year's presents
You can't afford to take them out for a company party
When a company earns two million dollars a year — you can't rent an office downtown and renovate it in your corporate design.
Installing a … kitchen at home costs 30 thousand pounds, and that's a few square meters
When I see in downtown San Francisco that a startup has renovated a whole floor for itself — I can imagine how much money was put into it
Because a million dollars is the annual salary of 5 decent employees with taxes + benefits, and that's it.
With what's left you can maybe renovate a garage, and even then line it with plain drywall and spray-paint the drywall
And the people who put money into businesses — they … don't give it away
The moment they see that you're a … “CREATOR” …, they'll … send you packing right away and won't give you a cent
They need you to bust your ass, and especially your people's
Preferably, if possible, … without paying them
And have them live in a barn
And … manage to sell some piece of … for enough to return them at least 20% a year on the invested money
That's all people with money really need
The only thing that helps the world is competition
Remove competition and it gets truly brutal, straight out of Orwell and Zamyatin
Competition makes it NECESSARY for things to be a little prettier
A little more pleasant
A little neater
Not for the sake of creation
But because otherwise you won't sell … and won't hit the capitalist quota
That, in fact, is the real engine of progress, of creativity and so on — the necessity of taking a piece of the market from a competitor by means of something
If that necessity didn't exist, all artists would at most be wandering the subway barefoot, selling their drawings on the cheapest paper
And under any political system
Yeah, I dream of going back to Dota
I just promised myself I won't play until I finish a few things
And I've already done almost everything on the time-consuming list
Just today I was thinking that any day now I'll be able to sit down and … play
Today I still can't, because I haven't finished what I have to
I just … got carried away in the end with automation at the agency
Today, for example, I finally finished this flow
1) I now have a fully custom Telegram CRM with a UI

Some of it manual, some of it pulled in, for example, from the requests on the website. The CRM pings me so that I ping clients, and offers me the results of micro-deep-researches and several ping options to choose from.

2) When I kick a lead over to “contract signed,” the lead drops into the “Clients” section. There the signed contract is automatically scanned, all the billing info is filled in + the first invoice is automatically issued and sent to the invoice storage and to me in Telegram.
3) All the documents for each client are stored and checked for the correct numbering format, de-conflicted

4) When a new client is created, workspaces in Instantly, domains, mailboxes and other accounts get created — automatically where possible, manually otherwise (the system pings me so I don't forget and won't let me press the “Done” button until everything is done).
5) When I press “done,” checks and tests run to confirm that everything about the client is known correctly and pings/works. Every webhook, every workspace.
6) The infrastructure automatically goes into warm-up and reports the warm-up status to me every day.

7) When 7 days of the paid period remain, an invoice flies out to the client from the bot. Another bot tracks incoming payments by the Company name from the billing details on the invoices, and if no payment came in — every day the bot … the client to transfer the money and share the payment confirmation.

Honestly I can't be bothered to describe it all, but there are dozens more elements. Smart rotation of mailboxes and checking them for spam health (I ended up building my own because it actually works, unlike that paid snake pit which only exposes your mailboxes to Google as a spammer's … because you use such services)
Even … contacts are semi-automated. Not fully, but for launching test hypotheses, chunks of contacts by particularly obvious criteria aren't hard to mine and sort onto shelves automatically
I don't understand what the problem could be in managing 24 people — that's one
Two — different leaders have different approaches to hiring
The second most likely fully explains the first =)
I hire people who are managed in a certain way, have certain values, etc.
Many of those who've poached my people can't manage them
They take them and … it doesn't work out
But it worked for me
It would most likely be the same the other way around
Plus we can dig further
10 million dollars on 24 people….
And how many dollars does the single biggest client bring in?
All of it?
Half?
Any of those answers fundamentally changes the meaning of management and the reading of any problem such a company runs into

I've seen many companies with 10 and even 50 million dollars in revenue from de facto 3 clients whom the founder brought in and handles, and the 100 people in the company do … who knows what and …, the real business there is done by 3 people.
De jure it's a 100-person company that can tell you something about managing a 100-person company
De facto they … don't know how to manage anyone
Because under management nothing is born except costs, and money is born where, in essence, there is no management.
That's just one angle to look from, and there are … more of them)

So if you drew the mathematical matrix of all possible variants, all companies are unique like snowflakes, even though at first glance they're hard to tell apart, since the words are the same and the structures identical
One company is simply someone's laundromat
The second company lives on a contract the father-in-law arranged out of love for his daughter
The third company lives on kickbacks
The fourth on grants
The fifth on market scraps (like those dev studios that take $1,000 projects from classifieds)
The sixth on a single star closer who got lucky 4 times and then once more invested the dough from his previous 4 lucky breaks correctly
The seventh… the eighth…. the hundred and fiftieth….
The number of people … doesn't matter at all in the end, just as much else that comes to mind offhand doesn't matter
I understand that I … some people really badly with my notes about vibe-coding.
But, first, this is a channel about vibe-coding.
Second, rather than sulk, let's make out instead!!!
So. This agonizing 24-hour development of mine is pushed forward not only by curiosity but also by a peculiar philosophical vision of the situation taking shape.

If the world throws people like you into the furnace, the most reliable way to come through it with dignity is to arrange a training for yourself in advance, as similar as possible to what the world will later test you on.

Your own trials are easier to pass: you set the rules yourself and understand what it's all for. They sound concrete — unlike the murky test program that the world hasn't even properly formulated yet.

My personally set trial for this year: I no longer do anything by hand that I can achieve through automation within a sane timeframe. And that is everything that repeats more than X times. I haven't settled on the size of that X yet, but it's unlikely to be much bigger than ten. So: if I intend to, or will be forced to, do anything not related to pleasure more than 10 times, then I must automate it once, whatever it takes, or not do it at all.
At the current stage this approach to life doesn't yet feel very comfortable, because although AI is developing … fast, it's still in deep beta.
Some things I could do by hand in five minutes, but coding their recurring implementation sometimes takes me 2 or even 4 days, and sometimes all of 10.
During those days I irritate people, lose some options, harm the processes of the moment.
However, if you work it out on a calculator, the damage from the lifestyle chosen for this year is far smaller than it seems, and the real upside can't be measured with any ruler.

Arithmetically it's tempting to think that 2, 4 and 10 days consist of a fairly small number of “five-minute slots.” There are a full 288 five-minute slots in one day. Think how much you can do! Okay, you also have to sleep, which leaves us 192 five-minute slots.

But an experienced user of life knows that 5 minutes of any work is never 5 minutes. It's 5 minutes of the task + double or triple kickback in the form of procrastination + energy lost switching between tasks + the slippage of reloading mental context + the resistance of entering flow if the task requires creativity.
Sometimes 5 minutes of work is 10 physical minutes.
And sometimes it's several hours, or even a whole day.
I'm sure everyone understands perfectly what I'm talking about and can recall recent tasks that “seemed like … nothing to do,” yet for some reason took an entire day.

There are “5-minute” tasks with extremely high viscosity: they stick like … to your feet. Invoices without data, email replacements without context, reconciling something against something, clarifications with elements of a game of telephone, “take a quick look and tell me in two words” — none of these are tasks, they're slime. It's easy to drown in them because they have no clear boundaries. A true slacker simply dies from each such task and rises again only tomorrow.
There are “5-minute” tasks that expose 100 other tasks that also need to be done in 5 minutes each, because without them the original one makes no sense.

Recently I was in the shower — and, languidly soaping the inside of my thigh, I realized what the main change on the map of society is right now. Something I'd started to feel back in '22 but couldn't quite catch.
Society is reaching escape velocity in the race for time.
Time has always been a relative parameter. Relative in many senses.
Relative to one event it drags, relative to another it flies.
Some people think thousands of times faster than others, yet live a biological span of comparable length. Does that mean one person lives a thousand times more life? Of course.

Two minutes in a plank is a small eternity. Two hours in a game where you're “one more match and then bed” is a small instant. Time expands where pain torments you and contracts where dopamine is being injected into the blood.

There is “clock time” and there is “attention time.” You can live eighty years with the light switched off inside, and then it will be a short life. Or you can live thirty, but with attention to reality so sharp that it's longer than several centuries.
The time of a person who knows how to say “no” is longer. Because he doesn't scatter his life on other people's wants. He literally buys his hours back by cutting off the costs expressed in time.

Interest and compound interest are the mathematics of time's relativity in money. A year for capital that grows is longer than a year for capital that sits. Same calendar, but a completely different physics of expected value (that is, a different trajectory of the future under the same calendar).

Time in relationships is relative too: one minute of silence after the phrase “I …” can drag on like the funeral of a one-night stand. And three hours of honest conversation can close years of internal drama.
And so … on…
So: the race for time has always existed. And it has been quite democratic — that is, bloody and cruel =)

When parents send a child to Harvard for insane money, they're buying a chance: for the child to gain additional relative life-time within the same biological span. Not hours on a dial, but time-as-opportunity: fewer dead ends, more doors, a higher growth rate.

One person starts from zero, another from ten million dollars. The first can grow, fight, get smarter, accelerate, but the statistics are cynical: in one lifetime he most often doesn't even reach the second one's starting line. And it isn't about “talent,” it's that their time has different purchasing power from the outset.

Life isn't only money, I know. But to give the system a shape you need convenient viewing angles. Cash is convenient because it's numbers everyone understands. All the other forms of this system you can construct yourself: a metric can be found for any emotion, but to do that effectively you need to be a lot more than what it takes to just feel the difference between “$0” and “$10,000,000.”
So here it is: the distance between people is now going to start growing at a … pace.

The Internet gave everyone equal access to knowledge, but didn't give equal access to discipline, attention and the ability to assemble knowledge into value, which significantly aggravated the inequality of time. AI will give many people access to acceleration, but won't give equal access to choosing the right goals. And that is a completely different sort of inequality. And even when access seems “equal,” the context isn't: one person has 2 hours a day and chaos in his head, another has a team, data and iron discipline.
AI will now amplify what the Internet started by an unthinkable factor.
The gap between people grows not because “some are smarter.” But because some learn to convert effort into a system on the fly, while others keep converting effort into fatigue.

People learning to vibe-code today aren't learning to write code — it's no longer the center of the digital universe. It was needed only so that the digital universe could be born at all out of a gas cloud of poorly combed zeros and ones. That is, code was the language of the primary assembly of infrastructure. Now the infrastructure is standing, and value is shifting five parsecs over — to setting tasks, designing processes and controlling quality.

Code is no longer the main skill, because code is the “how.” And the world is starting to pay for the “what” and the “why.” If you can formulate a task, bound it, check its reality, calculate the cost of an error — you're a god of the new world. You're the one who'll now kick open the bar door and order beer for everyone. If you can't — you're just a passenger in someone else's product. And you're the one paying for it, as a passenger, not being paid as before. Before, you were a piece of the driver, the fuel he ran on, expressed in the time available to you that he bought from you. Now your time is needed only by you, and only you will be able to convert it into benefits for yourself.

It's important to realize that those who are vibe-coding flat out right now are learning to live in this new world: where you don't “type characters,” you assemble a conveyor. You don't write code — you set up machines that stamp out results: emails, reports, invoices, deals, research, applied use of that research, content, products. Assemble it once — then it runs by itself and doesn't crap on your soul every Monday. You know EXACTLY what will happen in a week. If that stops satisfying you — you improve the system, and again you know EXACTLY what will happen in a week.

The especially talented will invent not “pieces of matter” but new tools and protocols: how people buy, how they learn, how they work, how they make decisions. That is, they'll reflash consumers' daily lives, offering better solutions than the consumer himself could come up with — who, if he could come up with something better, would have created it in the same place you did, for pennies.

The mass of people who in all seriousness are now “learning to code” with the help of vibe-coding, instead of learning to solve any of their own problems with automation, are the monkeys from the fable “The Monkey and the Spectacles.”

I remember how in childhood every neighborhood …, including those who couldn't string two words together, knew how to replace the thermal paste on a CPU to keep playing Duke Nukem over a cable (there was no Internet yet).
Now many of those … earn 30 thousand rubles as warehouse loaders — and keep replaying Diablo 2.
Many born after, say, 2005 have never laid eyes on that … thermal paste. And it doesn't stop them from looting $150k+ a year working as engineers at the best companies on the planet.
Writing code is smearing thermal paste on a processor.
Vibe-coding isn't coding instead of coders, it's everything except writing code.

It's the skill of designing interfaces. The skill of working with load. The skill of budgeting the start, the middle and the finish. The skill of scaling. The skill of switching, refusing, connecting and disconnecting.
WANTING AND CHOOSING.
You can list this … forever, and this … isn't such a small …. It's gold you have to manage to mine. It doesn't jump into your head by itself, and there's no fast track here.
It's the skill of breaking your own head and ceasing to think in actions, starting to think in systems. It used to be “Idea -> Effort -> Result.” Now only “Idea -> Conveyor -> Result” will be valued.

I once devoured those … BOOKS on the same principle. I doubt I liked every book I read. Read Freud — you want to cry. Read Nietzsche — you go mad. What's … pleasant about that? But I had to break my poor provincial head and force an enormous mass of meanings into it, to be figured out later. And every one of them came in handy.

I looked at rich and famous people, and listening to their speech, looking at the products of their lives, it was crystal clear: without the puzzle pieces you can't assemble the expensive puzzle. Only the cheap one with six micro-pieces from a Kinder Surprise, and even then only if there's a Kinder Surprise, and if it contains a puzzle and not some … Mickey Mouse.

Every automation, first, lets a person get smarter by that automation and then reproduce the needed pieces for the next task ten (and later a hundred) times faster. It's like learning not the answer but the way to obtain answers.
Second, it simply speeds things up. Because today I stop spending 5 minutes which, as it turned out, are never 5 minutes. And tomorrow I'll stop spending 50, which aren't 50 at all.

I think that starting tomorrow I'll begin to live a life several times longer than those who also try but lag behind. And billions of times longer than those who keep lowing at the caravan and poking a hoe at a rock.
This race isn't just announced, it's already underway. Participating isn't mandatory, but it's better to remember that the economy is a very sturdy condom.

90% of the condom gets grabbed with their greedy mitts by the top 1% of the world's racers while nobody's watching, and they … off into the sunset in the most souped-up cars. And the thickness of the remaining 10% of the rubber, how it thins as the leaders pull away from the chasers, and which side the rubber thins on — I don't think that needs explaining even to first-graders.
Only now a souped-up car can be assembled practically for free. You'll have to pay only with a heap of discomfort, patience, time and blood, but everyone has those resources.
Right now AI will add x10 to every racer who wants it. Tomorrow x100. The day after, x10,000 speed.
Which side of the condom you want to ride on, thick or thin — that's up to you.
But the mechanics these days are simple: either you build conveyors, or you go …:)
Yes, we don't run them; clients have to close the deals with the leads themselves
Over many, many years I've understood that if a client can't do that, there's no point in his existence in general.
Doing someone's entire business for them is a dubious responsibility that always leads to a dead end.
Normal people don't want that loss of control either, and rightly so
Especially now, in 2026. If I'm generating leads for people myself and closing them into money myself, then maybe I should just slip them my own product?:)))))

This is work on the quality of the service. Quality gives higher metrics. Higher metrics — better relationships with clients on average, longer partnerships, more completely … projects dragged at least somewhere, which again lengthens the partnership cycle, plus better word of mouth, etc. etc.
Our quality jumped tenfold in a year thanks to AI and automations
Right now that's the only way, in a falling market, not to stand still but even to grow somewhat
If we worked today the way we did in 2024, the agency would no longer exist
Well, more precisely, it would be living hand to mouth, like almost all agencies
It's just that the dweebs who run outreach agencies are usually satisfied with half a senior's corporate salary, and I'm not satisfied even with ten salaries:)
A million a year can still be pulled in, but only with … tooling; by hand you can't do absolutely anything anymore except scam clients
Unfortunately the tooling costs … money, so the check can't be lowered. I buy outreach from myself for the same ten grand
Because tens of millions of tokens and hundreds of domains and mailboxes + all the know-how for getting around blocks unfortunately don't come from …
But instant money is always … unless it's a hustle or a scheme. All my life I've counted on middle-to-long money in everything I do
Return in 6–9 months. B2B is a slow-moving thing, one …
They've dropped a lot, but I … 18/7 anyway
Time gets freed up not necessarily to be thrown in the trash
I don't understand people at all when they say they're now going to work like hell to earn enough to do nothing.
They won't earn it)
You can only earn as collateral damage

When a person isn't sleeping, they're doing something anyway. The world outside the window doesn't offer enough activities for a genuinely smart head. Walk around parks sniffing sunrises and sunsets nonstop? A person who can genuinely enjoy that long-term is hard to call an intellectual.

Building Google is doable too. Sergey Brin built it, after all;)
For my part I can only say that the amount of headache in this business is such that I see NO successful cases anywhere outside of Bomb, although in 12 years someone probably could have turned up

But on inspection they turned out to be scammers
In my world a scam isn't when they outright steal the money
But when for money they perform a set of motions in which a result could only come out by some transcendent, epochal miracle
In our business you really have to manage to knit thousands of different parameters into one ball
And then also survive the level of market resistance
Nobody loves lead gen
Everyone wants to kick lead gen in the …
With everything that follows
In most businesses they can't even tell you offhand why they survive. And mostly it's founders who, running around in a panic, knitted something together somewhere.
There is an alternative to lead gen, after all, since most companies have no lead gen and somehow exist, pay people salaries, grow.
Most often the fifth element is market fit + business model + the right fundraising
If all three components are …, it's like a stick you jam into the ground in Texas and oil gushes out, roughly
And the rest usually hustle through friends & family, jump onto some one fat client — in Russia it's usually some VTB24-like shit
And pray
Sometimes the prayer works for decades)
Criticizing anyone is useless. If right now a guy has the cash to travel, eat at restaurants, get into a new car, then well done to him.
In terms of interaction, people … are no different at all from an LLM, and an LLM that isn't trying at all)

To feel this right now, talk to some deep experts in their domain who long ago forgot that someone might not have a PhD in their subject. They sincerely believe they knew it all from the cradle, and everyone else isn't worthy of that knowledge.
For the full effect you need to talk to them precisely about their domain. Some narrowly specialized coder-founders are perfect for this.

Talking to such a person, you have to think hard about how to phrase the question so that he can answer it even somewhat intelligibly. It takes 10 or more attempts at the apparatus) With each attempt the risk of silence in reply increases.
No wonder Steve Wozniaks need Steve Jobses, so that their business team has more than two autists and more clients than a couple of childhood friends who did well =)
Lately I talk a lot with people who, before my recent leap in development smarts, wouldn't have talked to me at all.

God, how hard it is to make them simply answer some important question directly and completely. From some of them I'm trying to buy something, but it's incredibly hard to do, because they can't open their mouths and tell me in detail how their … specifically performs its function, and without that there's no point in buying — a vicious circle.

And that's me entertaining them as best I can, while an ordinary client wants to BE entertained) And even if he's entertained long and thoroughly enough, he'll still think about whether to transfer the money.

I have no doubt that even with … vibe-coding, in a scalable product business I need a technical co-founder. Not only because without him you can't scale load quickly, but because there's no time to deal with technology if sales are flying — you have to fundraise and … all over the world on a business mission, which pairs … with silent staring into a terminal.
However, in my memory the absolute majority of technical founders avoid sales/marketing/business co-founders in every way. Most likely out of disrespect.

So they sit on their technically perfect projects with 100 unique visitors a month on the site (95 of which are crawler bots), and … over forks and stars on GitHub, which don't bring in a … of commission)
